claims.text: High configurational entropy establishes a homogeneous, disordered state in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
The high-configurational-entropy state kinetically retards atomic diffusion.
Retarded atomic diffusion prevents surface segregation and phase separation during high-temperature service.
Preservation of homogeneous atomic mixing and short-range order is critical to nanoparticle stability.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform, atomically homogeneous elemental distribution.
Controlled post-synthesis annealing can subtly perturb atomic mixing relative to rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching preserves full atomic homogeneity.
Use of inert or controlled atmospheres minimizes extrinsic chemical effects during high-temperature exposure.
Atomic pair distribution function analysis, STEM-EDS, and XPS mapping can assess short-range chemical order, bulk elemental homogeneity, or surface composition.
High configurational entropy increases the activation barrier for atomic diffusion.
A higher diffusion activation barrier slows elemental segregation and phase separation.
Nanoparticles that remain atomically homogeneous after thermal treatment will show minimal phase separation and surface segregation.
Nanoparticles with reduced atomic homogeneity will undergo greater structural degradation than the rapidly quenched baseline.
Reduced atomic homogeneity will cause greater deterioration in catalytic or thermoelectric performance than in the baseline.
The proposed stabilization mechanism applies when constituent elements have similar atomic sizes and favorable mixing enthalpies.
The proposed mechanism may fail for systems containing highly disparate elements or when strong oxidation dominates degradation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the stabilizing state as homogeneous and disordered, but later treats retention of short-range chemical order as equivalent to homogeneity. Chemical short-range order and random homogeneous disorder are distinct structural concepts and can change independently.
